lessons.prologue: Before a single Roman road was built across Britain, dozens of proud Iron Age tribes farmed green valleys, crowned hilltops with giant earth ramparts, and twisted pure gold into gleaming neck rings. Step inside a smoky thatched roundhouse to discover how Celtic Britons really lived!
lessons.blurb: Before a single Roman road was built across Britain, dozens of proud Iron Age tribes farmed green valleys, crowned hilltops with giant earth ramparts, and twisted pure gold into gleaming neck rings. Step inside a smoky thatched roundhouse to discover how Celtic Britons really lived!

teacher_notes.primer: This opening enquiry introduces Years 3–4 pupils to Iron Age Celtic Britain (c. 500 BC – AD 43) before the Roman conquest. Pupils overturn the common misconception that pre-Roman Britons were "primitive cavemen" by exploring tribal kingdoms (Iceni, Catuvellauni, Brigantes), giant earthwork hillforts like Maiden Castle, clever chimney-free roundhouse engineering, Druid oral traditions, dazzling gold torcs and bronze shields, and cross-Channel trade alongside Julius Caesar's brief landings in 55 BC and 54 BC.

items.question: On a history timeline, what do the letters "BC" after a date stand for?
items.answer: Before Christ (years counted backwards before AD 1)
items.explanation: In BC dates, bigger numbers happened longer ago — so 500 BC came centuries before 55 BC!

items.question: On a history timeline, which happened earlier: 500 BC or AD 43?
items.explanation: All BC ("Before Christ") years happened before AD ("Anno Domini") years began.

items.question: Great Britain is surrounded completely by sea. What geographical word describes land surrounded by water?
items.explanation: Because Great Britain is an island, ancient visitors and armies had to cross the sea in wooden ships.

items.question: Which narrow stretch of sea separates southern England from France and mainland Europe?
items.explanation: On a clear day, white chalk cliffs can be seen across the narrowest part of the English Channel.

items.question: In which sunny southern European country is the ancient city of Rome located?
items.explanation: Rome began as a city in Italy shaped like a boot stretching into the warm Mediterranean Sea.

items.question: Why do historians call the period before the Romans arrived in Britain the "Iron Age"?
items.answer: Because people learned to heat and hammer iron to make strong tools and weapons
items.explanation: Iron ploughs, axes, and swords were stronger and sharper than earlier Stone Age or Bronze Age tools.

items.question: Before cars, trains, or paved roads existed, how did people carry heavy goods between Britain and Europe?
items.answer: By wooden sailing and rowing boats across rivers and seas
items.explanation: Water travel by river and sea was much faster for heavy cargo than dragging carts through muddy forests.

items.question: Which country lies directly across the English Channel to the south-east of England (called "Gaul" in ancient times)?
items.explanation: Ancient Romans called the lands of modern France and Belgium "Gaul".

items.question: If an ancient community never wrote down books or letters, how do archaeologists find out how they lived?
items.answer: By digging up artefacts, coins, bones, and building remains left in the ground
items.explanation: Objects left behind in soil and rivers give historians physical clues about everyday life long ago.

items.question: What everyday foods can farming families make when they grow fields of wheat and keep cows and sheep?
items.answer: Bread or porridge from wheat flour, plus milk, cheese, meat, and warm wool
items.explanation: Farming allowed ancient families to settle in permanent villages and store grain for winter.

vocab.definition: A circular Iron Age family home with woven clay walls, a central fire, and a tall cone-shaped thatched roof with no chimney.
A settlement built high on a hilltop and ringed with steep earth banks (ramparts), deep ditches, and wooden fences for protection.
Woven strips of bendy hazel wood (wattle) plastered with a sticky mixture of clay, mud, animal dung, and straw (daub) to make warm walls.
A heavy, twisted neck ring made of gold, silver, or bronze worn by wealthy Celtic rulers and warriors to show high status.
Powerful Celtic priests, judges, and teachers who memorised thousands of sacred laws and poems instead of writing books.

narrative_blocks.title: Tribes, Warriors & Giant Earth Hillforts
narrative_blocks.text:
[1.1] Before Roman soldiers arrived, green Britain belonged to **Iron Age Celts**. Britain had no single king, as **separate tribes** ruled their own lands. They included the **Iceni** [eye-SEE-nee] in the east, the **Catuvellauni** [kat-oo-vel-AW-nee] in the south, and the **Brigantes** [brig-AN-teez] in the north.

[1.2] Tribes protected cattle inside giant **hillforts** like **Maiden Castle** in Dorset. Steep earth **ramparts**, deep ditches, and wooden fences ringed the hilltop. In **55 BC** and **54 BC**, chariot warriors fought **Julius Caesar** until he sailed back.

narrative_blocks.title: Inside a Smoky Thatched Roundhouse
narrative_blocks.text:
[1.3] Most Celtic farming families lived inside circular homes called **roundhouses**. Builders wove hazel sticks into **wattle-and-daub** walls plastered with clay, mud, and straw. Above rose a cone **thatched roof** with **no chimney**, so wind could not blow sparks inside.

[1.4] Smoke from the central **hearth fire** drifted gently through the thatch. Rising woodsmoke cured meat in the rafters and chased away insects. Parents wove bright wool cloaks on tall wooden **looms**, while children turned heavy **quern stones** [KWURN] to grind wheat into flour.

narrative_blocks.title: Master Craftworkers, Druids & Sea Traders
narrative_blocks.text:
[1.5] **Iron Age** Britons were skilled craftworkers and storytellers, not rough savages. Smiths twisted pure gold ropes into heavy neck rings called **gold torcs**. They placed gleaming **bronze shields** in sacred rivers, while wise **Druids** memorised laws and prayers without writing books.

[1.6] Busy sea traders sailed wooden boats across the **English Channel**. Ships carried **Cornish tin**, iron, cattle hides, hunting dogs, and **wheat** to Europe. Rulers even minted **gold stater coins**, spreading news of Britain's riches straight to **Rome**!

tasks.starter: Looking closely at Source A, the steep earth banks and deep ditches helped protect a Celtic tribe because...
hints: Describe the steep chalk and earth banks (ramparts) and deep ditches ringing the hilltop.
Explain how climbing exhausting slopes slowed down attackers and cattle raiders.

tasks.model_answer: Looking closely at Source A, the steep earth banks and deep ditches helped protect a Celtic tribe because raiders had to scramble up exhausting chalk ramparts one ring after another. tasks.title: 2. Historical Investigation
tasks.question: Why did Iron Age builders make roundhouse roofs in a tall cone shape WITHOUT a chimney hole at the top?
tasks.starter: Iron Age builders cleverly gave their thatched roundhouses no chimney hole because...
hints: Explain the fire danger if wind blew through the door and drew hot sparks up through a chimney hole onto dry straw.
Describe two helpful jobs done by the slow-rising smoke inside the rafters (meat and insects!).
Explain how experimental archaeologists at Butser Ancient Farm tested this design when original Iron Age roofs rotted away long ago.
tasks.model_answer: Iron Age builders cleverly gave their thatched roundhouses no chimney hole because an open hole at the top would act like a wind tunnel, sucking glowing sparks from the central hearth fire straight into the dry straw roof! Instead, smoke seeped gently out through the thick cone-shaped thatch. As it drifted upwards, the smoke cured meat hanging in the rafters so food lasted all winter and drove away biting insects from the family below.

tasks.title: 3. Mission Challenge • The Big Question
tasks.question: Big Question: Who were the Iron Age Celts, and how did they live before the Roman legions arrived?
tasks.starter: Before the Roman legions arrived in AD 43, the Iron Age Celts were far from backward because...
hints: Explain how tribes like the Iceni and Brigantes organised farms and built giant hillforts such as Maiden Castle.
Give examples of clever Celtic homes (chimney-free roundhouses) and dazzling metalwork (gold torcs and bronze shields).
Weigh up why people once underestimated the Celts — pointing out that Druids memorised knowledge orally instead of leaving written books like the Romans.
tasks.model_answer: Before the Roman legions arrived in AD 43, the Iron Age Celts were far from backward because they were clever builders, skilled farmers, master smiths, and international sea traders. Proud tribes such as the Iceni, Catuvellauni, and Brigantes engineered giant earth hillforts like Maiden Castle and cosy wattle-and-daub roundhouses. Their smiths twisted pure gold into gleaming torcs, while ships traded Cornish tin, wheat, and gold stater coins across the English Channel. People only underestimated them later because Druids memorised laws by heart rather than writing books, leaving Romans to write the history!

By one single King of all Britain in London
By Egyptian pharaohs across the sea

quiz.a: By dozens of separate tribes each ruling their own lands
quiz.explanation: Iron Age Britain was not one united country; dozens of separate tribes such as the Iceni, Catuvellauni, and Brigantes ruled their own territories.

quiz.q: Which massive Iron Age hillfort in Dorset was ringed with steep earth ramparts and wooden fences?

quiz.q: In which two years did the Roman general Julius Caesar first land in Britain before sailing back to Gaul?
quiz.explanation: Julius Caesar crossed the Channel to Britain twice, in 55 BC and 54 BC, fighting Celtic chariot warriors before returning to Gaul.

quiz.question: Which Iron Age tribe lived in eastern Britain, while the Brigantes lived in the north?
quiz.q: Which Iron Age tribe lived in eastern Britain, while the Brigantes lived in the north?
quiz.explanation: The Iceni ruled lands in eastern Britain (East Anglia), the Catuvellauni lived in the south, and the Brigantes lived in the north.

quiz.question: How did steep earth ramparts, deep ditches, and wooden fences help defend an Iron Age hillfort?
quiz.q: How did steep earth ramparts, deep ditches, and wooden fences help defend an Iron Age hillfort?
options: They flooded the hilltop to sail warships
Attackers tired out climbing steep banks while defenders watched from above
They hid secret underground railway tunnels
They kept heat inside like a greenhouse
quiz.answer: Attackers tired out climbing steep banks while defenders watched from above
quiz.a: Attackers tired out climbing steep banks while defenders watched from above
quiz.explanation: Towering earth ramparts and deep ditches slowed down cattle raiders and gave defenders high ground.

quiz.question: What mixture was used to build the circular "wattle-and-daub" walls of an Iron Age roundhouse?
quiz.q: What mixture was used to build the circular "wattle-and-daub" walls of an Iron Age roundhouse?
options: Woven hazel branches plastered with clay, mud, and straw
Carved marble blocks and concrete cement
Fired red house bricks and glass windows
quiz.answer: Woven hazel branches plastered with clay, mud, and straw
quiz.a: Woven hazel branches plastered with clay, mud, and straw
quiz.explanation: Builders wove hazel branches into wattle panels and plastered them with sticky daub made of clay, mud, and straw.

quiz.question: Why did Iron Age builders deliberately make thatched roundhouse roofs WITHOUT a chimney hole?
quiz.q: Why did Iron Age builders deliberately make thatched roundhouse roofs WITHOUT a chimney hole?
options: They forgot where smoke came from
To keep pet birds trapped inside the rafters
So strong winds would not blow sparks into the dry thatch, and smoke cured meat
quiz.answer: So strong winds would not blow sparks into the dry thatch, and smoke cured meat
quiz.a: So strong winds would not blow sparks into the dry thatch, and smoke cured meat
quiz.explanation: Having no chimney prevented winds blowing sparks onto the dry straw roof, while rising smoke cured meat and drove away insects.

quiz.question: What heavy stone tool did Celtic children turn inside a roundhouse to grind wheat into flour?
quiz.q: What heavy stone tool did Celtic children turn inside a roundhouse to grind wheat into flour?
quiz.explanation: Families turned heavy stone quern stones by hand to grind wheat grain into flour, while wooden looms were used to weave woollen cloaks.

quiz.question: On what wooden frame did Celtic parents weave brightly patterned woollen cloaks inside the roundhouse?
quiz.q: On what wooden frame did Celtic parents weave brightly patterned woollen cloaks inside the roundhouse?
quiz.explanation: Parents wove brightly patterned woollen cloth and cloaks on tall upright wooden looms.

quiz.q: What two helpful jobs did rising woodsmoke from the central hearth fire do inside a roundhouse?
options: Powered iron steam engines and lit glass lamps
Cured meat hung in the rafters and chased away biting insects
Melted gold coins and baked red roof tiles
Watered indoor apple trees and cabbages

quiz.a: Cured meat hung in the rafters and chased away biting insects
quiz.explanation: Smoke drifting through the thatch smoked meat so it lasted through winter and kept insects out of the straw.

quiz.question: What was a Celtic "torc"?
quiz.q: What was a Celtic "torc"?
options: A heavy neck ring twisted from ropes of gold, silver, or bronze
A round stone used for grinding barley
An iron digging pick used on hillforts
quiz.answer: A heavy neck ring twisted from ropes of gold, silver, or bronze
quiz.a: A heavy neck ring twisted from ropes of gold, silver, or bronze
quiz.explanation: Celtic smiths twisted ropes of pure gold or bronze into heavy neck rings called torcs worn by leaders and warriors.

quiz.q: Why did the Iron Age Celts leave behind no written history books of their own?
options: They had no laws, poems, or stories to tell
Speaking aloud was forbidden inside hillforts
All their paper books washed across the Atlantic Ocean
Druids memorised thousands of laws, poems, and prayers instead of writing books

quiz.a: Druids memorised thousands of laws, poems, and prayers instead of writing books
quiz.explanation: Celtic religious leaders called Druids trained for years to memorise laws, poems, and prayers by heart rather than writing them down.

quiz.question: Where did Celtic Britons place precious decorated bronze shields like the Battersea Shield as gifts to water gods?
quiz.q: Where did Celtic Britons place precious decorated bronze shields like the Battersea Shield as gifts to water gods?

quiz.explanation: Ships crossed the English Channel trading Cornish tin, iron, cattle hides, hunting dogs, wheat, and gold stater coins.

lessons.prologue: In AD 43, hundreds of Roman warships appeared through the sea mist off the coast of Kent carrying 40,000 armored soldiers — followed weeks later by Emperor Claudius and trumpeting war elephants! Why did Claudius want Britain so badly, and what made the Roman army so tough to beat?

teacher_notes.primer: This enquiry investigates the causes and events of the Roman invasion of AD 43. Pupils distinguish between Emperor Claudius's personal motive (winning military glory to silence Roman senators who mocked his limp and stutter) and Rome's economic motives (silver, Cornish tin, lead, iron, wheat, and taxes). They then examine the professional Roman legionary's equipment and teamwork (caligae, lorica segmentata, scutum, testudo, bending pilum, and gladius) before following General Aulus Plautius's landing at Richborough, the Battle of the Medway against Caratacus, and Claudius's dramatic entry into Camulodunum (Colchester) with war elephants.

narrative_blocks.title: Britain's Riches & Claudius's Need for Glory
narrative_blocks.text:
[2.1] In **AD 41**, nervous **Emperor Claudius** [KLAW-dee-us] took power in Rome. Powerful Roman **senators** doubted him because he walked with a **limp** and spoke with a **stutter**. Having never led an army, Claudius needed **military glory** in **AD 43**.

[2.2] Conquering Britain also promised rich underground mines of **silver**, **Cornish tin**, **lead**, and **iron** for coins, pipes, and weapons. Southern farms grew golden **wheat** for troops, and conquered tribes would pay heavy Roman **taxes**.

narrative_blocks.title: The Unstoppable Roman War Machine
narrative_blocks.text:
[2.3] Full-time Roman **legionaries** marched **20 miles a day** in hobnailed **caligae** [KAL-ih-guy] sandals. They wore flexible iron strip armour called **lorica segmentata** [lor-EE-kuh seg-men-TAH-tuh]. Under arrow fire, troops locked curved **scutum** [SKOO-tum] shields into a **testudo** [tes-TOO-doh] ("tortoise") formation.

[2.4] Legionaries trained daily to fight as one calm team. First, they hurled a bending iron javelin called a **pilum** [PEE-lum] to ruin enemy shields. Next, soldiers stepped close behind their shield wall, stabbing with a short **gladius** [GLAD-ee-us] sword.

narrative_blocks.title: Landing at Richborough & Elephants at Camulodunum
narrative_blocks.text:
[2.5] In **AD 43**, General **Aulus Plautius** [AW-lus PLAW-tee-us] sailed over with **four legions** — around **40,000** soldiers. Troops landed at **Richborough in Kent**, dug strong ditches, and marched inland. In a fierce two-day battle at the **River Medway**, Rome defeated brave **Caratacus** [ka-RAT-uh-kus].

[2.6] Plautius waited near the River Thames until **Emperor Claudius** arrived in person with towering **war elephants** that terrified Celtic horses! Claudius marched proudly into **Camulodunum** [kam-yoo-loh-DOO-num] (**Colchester**), winning eleven kings' surrender and turning southern Britain into a Roman **province**.

tasks.question: Look at the marble statue of Emperor Claudius in Source A. Why did Claudius want Romans to see him as a mighty conqueror?

tasks.title: 2. Historical Investigation
tasks.question: Explain TWO reasons why Emperor Claudius invaded Britain in AD 43: one personal reason, and one reason about Britain's riches.
tasks.starter: Emperor Claudius invaded Britain in AD 43 for two big reasons. First, Claudius personally needed...
hints: Personal reason: Explain why Roman senators doubted Claudius (his limp, stutter, and lack of army experience) and how conquering Britain would win respect.
Riches reason: List the valuable metals and farm goods Rome wanted from Britain (silver, Cornish tin, lead, iron, wheat, and taxes).
Link this to Source D — why did General Aulus Plautius wait near the Thames so Claudius could personally march into Camulodunum with war elephants?
tasks.model_answer: Emperor Claudius invaded Britain in AD 43 for two big reasons. First, Claudius personally needed military glory because powerful Roman senators mocked his limp and stutter and doubted a ruler who had never led soldiers. Second, Rome wanted Britain's rich natural resources, including silver for coins, lead for water pipes, Cornish tin, iron, golden wheat to feed the army, and new taxes from conquered tribes. That is why General Aulus Plautius waited by the Thames so Claudius could arrive in person with war elephants and claim the triumph at Camulodunum!

tasks.title: 3. Mission Challenge • The Big Question
tasks.question: Big Question: Why did Emperor Claudius send 40,000 Roman soldiers and war elephants across the sea in AD 43?
tasks.starter: Emperor Claudius succeeded in conquering southern Britain in AD 43 because Rome arrived prepared with...
hints: Show the massive scale of the AD 43 invasion under General Aulus Plautius (four legions — 40,000 soldiers landing at Richborough).
Explain how professional legionary training, armour, bending pilum javelins, and locked testudo shields overcame separate British tribes.
Use Cassius Dio (Source D) to show that even nervous soldiers who feared sailing "outside the known world" succeeded through planning, supply bases, and Claudius's war elephants at Camulodunum.
tasks.model_answer: Emperor Claudius succeeded in conquering southern Britain in AD 43 because Rome arrived prepared to stay rather than just raid and leave. General Aulus Plautius landed a huge force of 40,000 full-time troops at Richborough in Kent and built strong supply ditches right away. On the battlefield at the River Medway, disciplined legionaries wearing lorica segmentata used bending pilum javelins, short gladius swords, and locked testudo shields to defeat Caratacus's part-time tribal warriors. Finally, Claudius arrived with terrifying war elephants to capture Camulodunum, winning eleven kings' surrender and turning southern Britain into a permanent Roman province.

lessons.prologue: Seventeen years after Claudius's invasion, Roman Britain nearly collapsed in flames! Enraged by broken Roman promises and cruel treatment, Queen Boudicca of the Iceni united rebel tribes and burned three Roman towns into red ash — before facing 10,000 Roman legionaries in a narrow valley along Watling Street.
lessons.blurb: Seventeen years after Claudius's invasion, Roman Britain nearly collapsed in flames! Enraged by broken Roman promises and cruel treatment, Queen Boudicca of the Iceni united rebel tribes and burned three Roman towns into red ash — before facing 10,000 Roman legionaries in a narrow valley along Watling Street.

teacher_notes.primer: This enquiry examines the most dramatic uprising in Roman Britain: Boudicca's Rebellion of AD 60–61. Pupils investigate why King Prasutagus's peaceful will to Emperor Nero was betrayed by greedy Roman officials, provoking Queen Boudicca of the Iceni and the neighbouring Trinovantes to rise up while Governor Suetonius Paulinus was campaigning far away in Anglesey. Pupils connect written accounts (Tacitus) with physical archaeology (the scorching red clay "destruction layer" beneath Colchester, London, and St Albans) before analysing why 10,000 disciplined legionaries defeated Boudicca's huge army in a narrow wooded valley at the Battle of Watling Street.

objectives.objective: Explain why broken Roman promises after King Prasutagus's death caused Queen Boudicca and the Iceni to rebel in AD 60.
objectives.primer: Unpack Prasutagus's will to Emperor Nero, stolen lands, sudden loan demands, and the flogging of Boudicca.
objectives.question: Why did Rome's treatment of a friendly ally like the Iceni turn peaceful tribes into fierce rebels?

objectives.objective: Describe how Boudicca burned Camulodunum, Londinium, and Verulamium, and how the "red clay destruction layer" proves it.
objectives.primer: Use the map (Anglesey vs East Anglia) and explain how archaeologists find burnt red clay, ash, and melted pottery under London.
objectives.question: How do archaeologists digging beneath modern London know how fiercely Boudicca's fires burned?

objectives.objective: Analyse why Suetonius Paulinus's 10,000 legionaries defeated Boudicca's much larger army at the Battle of Watling Street.
objectives.primer: Focus on terrain (narrow wooded valley), tight Roman wedges, squashed Celtic swords, and the ring of family wagons behind.
objectives.question: Why did a narrow wooded valley and parked family wagons turn Boudicca's huge numbers into a trap?

source_context.Source A: Boudicca left no written diary, so her story comes from Roman writers like Tacitus, whose father-in-law Agricola served as a young officer in Britain during the revolt. **Hinge Question:** Why is it surprising that a Roman writer like Tacitus admitted Roman officers acted greedily and unfairly?
source_context.Source B: When Boudicca attacked Camulodunum in AD 60, the town had no stone city wall yet, so afterwards Rome surrounded Colchester with thick stone walls and the Balkerne Gate. **Hinge Question:** What does building massive stone gates AFTER AD 61 tell us about how badly Boudicca shocked the Romans?
source_context.Source C: Governor Suetonius Paulinus and his legions were hundreds of miles north-west on Anglesey when Boudicca rose up, leaving south-east towns undefended. **Hinge Question:** Looking at Source C, how did the straight Roman road of Watling Street help Suetonius respond?
source_context.Source D: Deep beneath modern London streets lies a 40-centimetre band of burnt red clay, ash, and melted coins from AD 60, while above ground Rome rebuilt Londinium inside stone walls. **Hinge Question:** How do burnt red clay underground AND stone walls at Tower Hill work together to prove Tacitus's story?

items.question: Why did Iron Age thatched roundhouses have NO chimney hole in the roof?
items.answer: So wind could not blow sparks into the straw thatch, and rising smoke cured meat
items.explanation: Leaving out a chimney kept sparks safe and preserved meat hanging in the rafters.

items.question: Why did the Iron Age Celts leave no written history books of their own?
items.answer: Because Druids memorised laws, poems, and prayers by heart instead of writing books
items.explanation: Because Britons did not write books, written accounts of Roman Britain came from Roman authors.

items.question: Which Roman Emperor ordered the AD 43 invasion of Britain to win military glory and seize British metals?
items.explanation: Claudius wanted a famous triumph to silence doubting Roman senators plus silver, tin, lead, iron, and wheat.

items.question: What was the Roman "testudo" formation, and what curved shield did soldiers lock together to make it?
items.answer: The "tortoise" formation, made by locking curved rectangular scutum shields in front and overhead
items.explanation: Locked scutum shields formed an arrow-proof tortoise shell for advancing legionaries.

items.question: How far did professional Roman legionaries march each day in their hobnailed caligae sandals?
items.explanation: Daily 20-mile route marches made Roman legionaries fit, fast, and disciplined.

items.question: Where in Kent did General Aulus Plautius land 40,000 Roman troops in AD 43?
items.explanation: Plautius landed four legions and auxiliaries at Richborough in Kent before marching to the River Medway.

items.question: Which tribal capital (modern Colchester) did Emperor Claudius enter with war elephants in AD 43?
items.explanation: Camulodunum became Rome's proud showcase settlement in south-east Britain.

current_items.question: Whose death in AD 60 led Roman officials to break their promise and seize Iceni lands in East Anglia?
current_items.explanation: Prasutagus left half his wealth to Emperor Nero and half to his daughters, but greedy officials seized everything.

current_items.question: Where was Roman Governor Suetonius Paulinus campaigning when Boudicca's rebellion first broke out?
current_items.answer: Far away on Anglesey in north Wales
current_items.explanation: Because the main legions were hundreds of miles away in Anglesey, south-eastern towns were left poorly defended.

current_items.question: Name the THREE Roman towns burned to the ground by Queen Boudicca's rebel army in AD 60.
current_items.explanation: All three towns burned so fiercely they left a scorching red clay destruction layer underground.

current_items.question: What clue do archaeologists still dig up beneath modern London streets proving Boudicca burned Londinium?
current_items.answer: A scorching red clay "destruction layer" containing ash, blackened coins, and melted pottery
current_items.explanation: Fierce heat baked clay house walls bright red deep beneath today's pavements.

current_items.question: Why did Suetonius Paulinus's 10,000 legionaries beat Boudicca's huge army at the Battle of Watling Street in AD 61?
current_items.answer: A narrow wooded valley squashed the Britons together, Roman wedges pushed forward, and family wagons trapped them behind
current_items.explanation: Clever battlefield choice and disciplined Roman wedges overcame huge rebel numbers.

narrative_blocks.title: Broken Roman Promises to the Iceni
narrative_blocks.text:
[3.1] At first, Rome let friendly British rulers keep their thrones. In **East Anglia**, **King Prasutagus** [praz-oo-TAY-gus] of the **Iceni** stayed a peaceful ally of Rome. Dying in **AD 60**, he left half his wealth to **Emperor Nero** and half to his two daughters.

[3.2] Greedy Roman officials cruelly broke that promise at once! Soldiers marched in, **seized Iceni lands**, and demanded heavy Roman **loans** and taxes back. When **Queen Boudicca** [BOO-dik-uh] protested, officers had her **flogged** and **mistreated her daughters**.

narrative_blocks.title: Three Roman Towns Burn to Red Clay
narrative_blocks.text:
[3.3] Riding tall in her wooden war **chariot**, **Queen Boudicca** united the **Iceni**, the **Trinovantes** [trin-oh-VAN-teez], and angry neighbours. Roman Governor **Suetonius Paulinus** [swee-TOH-nee-us paw-LY-nus] was hundreds of miles away in **Anglesey** in north Wales! Rebels attacked **Camulodunum** (**Colchester**) first and burned its Roman temple.

[3.4] Next, Boudicca's huge army torched busy **Londinium** [lun-DIN-ee-um] (**London**) and **Verulamium** [ver-oo-LAY-mee-um] (**St Albans**). Burning timber shops baked into a scorching **red clay destruction layer**. Even today, **archaeologists** digging deep under London still find blackened coins and melted pots!

narrative_blocks.title: Showdown at the Battle of Watling Street (AD 61)
narrative_blocks.text:
[3.5] In **AD 61**, **Suetonius Paulinus** marched down **Watling Street** with **10,000** legionaries. Outnumbered, he chose a **narrow wooded valley** to guard his sides. Behind the field, confident Iceni families parked a **ring of wooden wagons** to watch.

[3.6] Charging Britons were squashed together so they could barely swing long swords. Marching in **tight wedges**, Romans hurled javelins and pinned rebels against their own wagons. Rome won, Boudicca died soon after, and **Londinium** was rebuilt inside **stone walls**.

tasks.question: Read Tacitus's words in Source A. What had King Prasutagus hoped would happen when he died, and what did Roman officials actually do?

tasks.model_answer: Looking closely at Source A, Tacitus explains that King Prasutagus hoped to protect his family, yet Roman officials broke his peaceful will as soon as he died. Instead of honouring his gift to Emperor Nero, greedy officers plundered Iceni homes, stole nobles’ lands, and mistreated Boudicca and her daughters, sparking the AD 60 rebellion.

tasks.title: 2. Historical Investigation
tasks.question: Boudicca had a much larger army than Suetonius Paulinus! Why did her rebellion still fail at Watling Street in AD 61?
tasks.starter: Even though Boudicca had far more warriors, her army lost the Battle of Watling Street because...
hints: Explain how Suetonius Paulinus cleverly used the landscape by choosing a narrow wooded valley that protected his sides.
Describe what happened when the Britons charged into the narrow funnel (squashed long swords vs tight Roman wedges).
Explain the tragic mistake made at the back of the British army with their ring of family wooden wagons.
tasks.model_answer: Even though Boudicca had far more warriors, her army lost the Battle of Watling Street because Governor Suetonius Paulinus chose the battlefield brilliantly. He lined up his 10,000 disciplined legionaries inside a narrow wooded valley so the huge British crowd could not surround his sides. When the Britons charged into that tight funnel, they got squashed together so closely that warriors could barely swing their long slashing swords! Advancing calmly in tight wedges after hurling their javelins, the Romans pushed the rebels backward until they were trapped against their own parked ring of wooden family wagons.

tasks.title: 3. Mission Challenge • The Big Question
tasks.question: Big Question: Why did Queen Boudicca lead a huge rebellion against Rome in AD 60, and why did it fail?
tasks.starter: Queen Boudicca's rebellion in AD 60 was caused by cruel Roman greed, and afterwards it changed Roman Britain by...
hints: Summarise the causes: broken promises to King Prasutagus and Emperor Nero, stolen Iceni lands, heavy loans, and mistreatment of Boudicca and her daughters.
Trace the climax: burning Camulodunum, Londinium, and Verulamium while Suetonius was in Anglesey, followed by defeat at Watling Street.
Explain the lasting consequences — rebuilding Colchester and Londinium inside mighty stone walls (Sources B & D) and governing British tribes more carefully so another revolt would not erupt.
tasks.model_answer: Queen Boudicca's rebellion in AD 60 was caused by cruel Roman greed when officials betrayed King Prasutagus's will to Emperor Nero, stole Iceni lands, demanded loans back, and flogged Boudicca. Taking advantage of Governor Suetonius campaigning far away in Anglesey, Boudicca united angry tribes and burned Camulodunum, Londinium, and Verulamium into a red clay destruction layer. Although 10,000 Roman legionaries won the Battle of Watling Street in AD 61 using a narrow wooded valley and tight wedges, Rome learned a big lesson — rebuilding Colchester and Londinium inside mighty stone walls and treating friendly British leaders more fairly.

lessons.prologue: In AD 122, Emperor Hadrian ordered Roman soldiers to build a 73-mile stone wall right across northern Britain from sea to sea. Buried in wet mud and carved onto stone tombstones, amazing clues reveal birthday parties, woollen socks, and soldiers from Europe, Syria, and North Africa guarding the cold frontier!
lessons.blurb: In AD 122, Emperor Hadrian ordered Roman soldiers to build a 73-mile stone wall right across northern Britain from sea to sea. Buried in wet mud and carved onto stone tombstones, amazing clues reveal birthday parties, woollen socks, and soldiers from Europe, Syria, and North Africa guarding the cold frontier!

teacher_notes.primer: This enquiry takes pupils to Rome's north-west frontier from AD 122 onwards. Pupils discover why Emperor Hadrian constructed a 73-mile (80 Roman mile) stone barrier between the River Tyne and the Solway Firth — not as an impenetrable seal, but as a controlled customs and military zone punctuated by milecastles, turrets, and 16 garrison forts like Housesteads. Using the anaerobic Vindolanda ink tablets (Tab. Vindol. II 291 & 346) and epigraphic tombstones at Burgh-by-Sands and Arbeia (RIB 1064 & 1065), pupils uncover both intimate domestic life and the remarkable multi-continental diversity of Roman Britain's frontier communities.

narrative_blocks.title: 73 Miles of Stone From Sea to Sea (AD 122)
narrative_blocks.text:
[4.1] In **AD 122**, **Emperor Hadrian** visited Britain and ordered a stone **frontier** wall across the north. **Hadrian's Wall** ran **73 miles** (**80 Roman miles**) from **Wallsend** on the River Tyne to **Bowness-on-Solway**, dividing Roman Britain from **Caledonia** [kal-ih-DOH-nee-uh] (modern Scotland).

[4.2] At every Roman mile stood a guarded stone gatehouse called a **milecastle** to stop cattle raids and collect border **taxes**. Backed by **16** large forts like **Housesteads**, soldiers even used communal stone **latrines** flushed clean by rainwater channels!

[4.2] At every Roman mile stood a guarded stone gatehouse called a **milecastle** to stop cattle raids and collect border **taxes**. Backed by **16** large forts like **Housesteads**, soldiers even used communal stone **latrines** flushed clean by rainwater channels!

narrative_blocks.title: Postcards in the Mud: The Vindolanda Tablets
narrative_blocks.text:
[4.3] Just south of the Wall stood **Vindolanda Fort** [vin-doh-LAN-duh]. There, wet, **oxygen-free mud** **preserved** hundreds of thin **wooden ink tablets** from around **AD 100** without rotting.

[4.4] On one tablet, **Claudia Severa** [KLAW-dee-uh seh-VAIR-uh] invited her friend **Sulpicia Lepidina** to a **birthday party** on 11 September — the oldest surviving **Latin handwriting by a woman**! Another tablet lists a parcel for a chilly soldier: **woollen socks**, two pairs of **sandals**, and two pairs of **underpants**.

narrative_blocks.title: Soldiers & Families From Across the Roman Empire
narrative_blocks.text:
[4.5] **Auxiliary** regiments from **three continents** — Europe, the Middle East, and **North Africa** — guarded Hadrian's Wall. **Batavian** soldiers from Europe, **Syrian archers**, and North African **Aurelian Moors** at **Burgh-by-Sands** all patrolled the windy northern border.

[4.6] Busy civilian towns called **vici** [WEE-kee] grew outside fort gates where families and shopkeepers lived. At **Arbeia Fort** [ar-BAY-uh] (South Shields), carved tombstones honour **Barates** [ba-RAH-teez] from **Syria**, his British **Catuvellauni** wife **Regina**, and young **Victor** from **Mauretania** in North Africa.

tasks.question: Why did Emperor Hadrian order a 73-mile stone wall with milecastle gates and 16 forts across northern Britain in AD 122?
tasks.starter: Emperor Hadrian ordered his legions to build a 73-mile stone wall across northern Britain in AD 122 because...
hints: Describe where the Wall ran (73 miles from Wallsend to Bowness-on-Solway) separating Roman Britain from Caledonia.
Explain the two main jobs of the guarded milecastle gates: stopping northern raids and collecting taxes from traders.

tasks.model_answer: Emperor Hadrian ordered his legions to build a 73-mile stone wall across northern Britain in AD 122 because he wanted to protect Roman Britain from raids out of Caledonia and control everyone crossing the border. Stretching from Wallsend to Bowness-on-Solway, the Wall had a guarded milecastle gate every Roman mile, two watchtowers in between, and 16 forts like Housesteads behind it. Rather than blocking people completely, milecastle gates let peaceful farmers and merchants pass through once soldiers checked their goods and collected Roman taxes.

tasks.title: 3. Mission Challenge • The Big Question
tasks.question: Big Question: Why did Emperor Hadrian build a 73-mile stone wall across northern Britain, and who guarded it?
tasks.starter: Archaeological clues from Vindolanda and Arbeia prove that Rome's northern frontier was home to a remarkably diverse community because...
hints: Name auxiliary troops from across the Empire: European Batavians, Syrian archers, and North African Aurelian Moors at Burgh-by-Sands.
Use the Arbeia Fort tombstones of Syrian trader Barates, his British wife Regina, and North African freedman Victor as solid proof.
Conclude how women, children, traders, and freed people in the vici towns show the frontier was far more than an all-male army camp.
tasks.model_answer: Archaeological clues from Vindolanda and Arbeia prove that Rome's northern frontier was home to a remarkably diverse community drawn from three continents — Europe, the Middle East, and North Africa. Auxiliary regiments included Batavians from the Netherlands, Syrian archers, and North African Aurelian Moors at Burgh-by-Sands. Outside the forts in busy vici towns, families and merchants settled too: Vindolanda's wooden letters reveal commanders' wives like Claudia Severa, while carved tombstones at Arbeia honour Barates from Syria, his British wife Regina from the Catuvellauni tribe, and Victor, a freedman from Mauretania in North Africa.

lessons.prologue: Roman engineers laid 10,000 miles of straight stone roads, piped fresh water into steaming bathhouses like Aquae Sulis, and heated dolphin-mosaic villas from underneath! Yet out in the countryside, did life really change for everyone?

teacher_notes.primer: This Change & Continuity enquiry explores the urban and technological revolution of Roman Britain alongside deep rural continuity. Pupils examine groma-surveyed cambered stone highways, planned towns with forums, basilicas, and amphitheatres (Caerleon), aqueduct water engineering, Aquae Sulis bathhouses, and hypocaust pilae heating. Crucially, Act 3 balances elite villas like Fishbourne Palace and imported Mediterranean foods (grapes, cherries, walnuts, garum) against archaeological reality: roughly 90% of Britons remained rural farmers living in thatched roundhouses while paying Roman taxes.

source_context.Source A: Using a wooden sighting tool called a groma, Roman engineers laid 10,000 miles of stone roads with curved surfaces and side ditches so rainwater ran straight off. **Hinge Question:** Why was building 10,000 miles of all-weather stone roads essential for keeping Roman control over Britain?
source_context.Source B: Major Roman towns and fortress settlements built oval stone amphitheatres where up to 6,000 spectators cheered gladiator bouts and parades. **Hinge Question:** Why did Roman governors and wealthy town leaders pay for free gladiator shows inside stone amphitheatres?
source_context.Source C: Public bathhouses like Aquae Sulis and wealthy villas used hypocaust heating: enslaved workers stoked a wood furnace so hot air flowed between brick tile stacks under the floor. **Hinge Question:** Who did the hard, smoky work needed to keep luxurious Roman bathhouses and villa floors warm?
source_context.Source D: Wealthy leaders decorated stone villas like Fishbourne Palace with mosaic floors, while almost nine out of ten country Britons kept living in thatched roundhouses. **Hinge Question:** Does a grand mosaic floor at Fishbourne Palace prove that EVERY family in Roman Britain lived in luxury?

narrative_blocks.title: Straight Stone Roads & Bustling Market Forums
narrative_blocks.text:
[5.1] Before Rome arrived, Britons travelled slowly along muddy dirt tracks. Roman surveyors used a wooden sighting **groma** [GROH-muh] to lay **10,000 miles** of dead-straight stone roads. Gently curved (**cambered**) paving stones and deep **side ditches** drained rainwater so carts rolled smoothly in all weathers.

[5.2] Where major highways met, Romans built walled grid towns around an open market **forum** and a **basilica** [buh-SIL-ih-kuh] town hall. Nearby, oval stone **amphitheatres** like **Caerleon** [kar-LEE-on] in South Wales seated cheering crowds for **gladiator** shows.

narrative_blocks.title: Aqueducts, Steam Baths & Underfloor Heating
narrative_blocks.text:
[5.3] Stone **aqueducts** and underground **lead pipes** carried fresh spring water into **Roman** towns, fountains, sewers, and **bathhouses** like **Aquae Sulis** [AK-wee SOO-lis] (**Bath**). Townsfolk visited the noisy public baths daily to exercise, chat, and wash.

[5.4] Bathhouses and rich homes used **hypocaust** [HY-poh-kawst] underfloor heating. Enslaved workers stoked a wood furnace so hot air blew between brick **pilae** [PEE-ly] stacks. Bathers rubbed on **olive oil**, then scraped oil and dirt off with a curved bronze **strigil** [STRIJ-il].

narrative_blocks.title: Dolphin Mosaics vs Countryside Roundhouses
narrative_blocks.text:
[5.5] In peaceful southern Britain, wealthy leaders built grand stone country **villas** like **Fishbourne Palace** in Sussex. Craftspeople pressed thousands of tiny coloured stone **tesserae** [TESS-er-ee] cubes into wet mortar to make **mosaic** floors. Rich diners tasted new foods like **grapes**, **cherries**, **walnuts**, and salty **garum** [GA-rum] fish sauce.

[5.6] Yet life did not change equally for rural **British** farmers. Across the countryside, almost **nine out of ten Britons** kept farming in smoky **thatched roundhouses** and speaking Celtic while paying **Roman taxes**.

tasks.title: 2. Historical Investigation
tasks.question: How did Roman engineers build roads and water systems that transformed travel and hygiene in British towns?
tasks.starter: Roman engineers transformed travel and town hygiene across Britain by building...
hints: Explain how surveyors used a groma to lay 10,000 miles of straight, cambered stone roads with side ditches.
Describe how stone aqueducts and lead pipes carried fresh spring water into fountains, sewers, and bathhouses like Aquae Sulis.
Link faster all-weather roads to both military control (moving legions fast) and booming trade in town forums.
tasks.model_answer: Roman engineers transformed travel and town hygiene across Britain by building 10,000 miles of stone highways and clever water networks. Using a groma sighting tool, soldiers built dead-straight roads with cambered surfaces and side ditches so rainwater ran off, letting legions and merchant carts reach town forums in all weathers. Meanwhile, stone aqueducts and underground lead pipes carried clean spring water into street fountains, flushing sewers, and steaming public bathhouses like Aquae Sulis, where bathers scraped off olive oil and dirt with a curved bronze strigil.

tasks.title: 3. Mission Challenge • The Big Question
tasks.question: Big Question: How did Roman roads, bathhouses, and stone towns transform everyday life in Britain?
tasks.starter: Roman rule brought dramatic changes to Britain's towns and wealthy homes, yet everyday life did not change equally for everyone because...
hints: Describe the big changes in towns and rich villas: 10,000 miles of stone roads, forums, Aquae Sulis baths, hypocaust heating, mosaics, and new foods.
Explain the big continuity: almost nine out of ten Britons carried on farming in countryside thatched roundhouses and speaking Celtic.
Explain how even countryside farmers in roundhouses still felt Roman rule through Roman roads and paying Roman taxes.
tasks.model_answer: Roman rule brought dramatic changes to Britain's towns and wealthy homes, yet everyday life did not change equally for everyone. For town-dwellers and rich tribal leaders in villas like Fishbourne Palace, life was transformed by 10,000 miles of stone roads, bustling forums, aqueduct water, steaming bathhouses like Aquae Sulis, hypocaust heating, dolphin mosaics, and foods like cherries and garum. However, almost nine out of ten ordinary Britons carried on farming in the countryside inside thatched timber roundhouses and speaking Celtic languages — though even they had to grow extra grain to pay Roman taxes!

lessons.prologue: By AD 410, raiders struck every coast and Emperor Honorius told Britain's towns they must defend themselves! Families buried chests of glittering silver underground as bathhouses crumbled — yet from London and straight A-roads to our ABC alphabet, July, apples, and rabbits, Roman clues still surround us every single day.
lessons.blurb: By AD 410, raiders struck every coast and Emperor Honorius told Britain's towns they must defend themselves! Families buried chests of glittering silver underground as bathhouses crumbled — yet from London and straight A-roads to our ABC alphabet, July, apples, and rabbits, Roman clues still surround us every single day.

teacher_notes.primer: This capstone enquiry brings 367 years of Roman rule in Britain to a close around AD 410 and evaluates Rome's enduring legacy. Pupils examine why legions were withdrawn (Picts, Scotti, Angles, and Saxons raiding Britain while Visigoths attacked Italy, leading to Emperor Honorius's AD 410 rescript recorded by Zosimus), what archaeological silver hoards (Hoxne and Mildenhall) and decaying bathhouses reveal about post-Roman uncertainty, and how Roman place-names (Londinium, castra/-chester), highways, the Latin ABC alphabet, Roman numerals, the 12-month calendar, Christianity, and introduced plants and animals still shape modern Britain.

items.question: In what year did Emperor Claudius invade Britain to make it part of the Roman Empire?
items.explanation: Four Roman legions landed in AD 43, beginning nearly 370 years of Roman rule in Britain.

items.question: Which Iceni queen burned Colchester, London, and St Albans during her AD 60–61 rebellion?
items.explanation: Queen Boudicca led a fierce rebellion before her defeat at the Battle of Watling Street.

items.question: Why did Emperor Hadrian build a 73-mile wall across northern Britain in AD 122?
items.answer: To stop northern raids from Caledonia and collect taxes at guarded milecastle gates
items.explanation: Hadrian's Wall controlled the northern frontier from Wallsend to Bowness-on-Solway.

items.question: What famous piece of writing by Claudia Severa survived in wet mud at Vindolanda Fort?
items.answer: A wooden ink birthday party invitation — the oldest surviving Latin handwriting by a woman
items.explanation: Written around AD 100, Tablet 291 invited her friend Sulpicia Lepidina to her birthday celebration.

items.question: From which three continents did auxiliary soldiers come to guard Hadrian's Wall?
items.answer: Europe, the Middle East, and North Africa
items.explanation: Batavians, Syrian archers, and North African Aurelian Moors all served along the northern frontier.

items.question: What wooden sighting tool helped Roman surveyors build 10,000 miles of straight stone roads?
items.explanation: Surveyors used a wooden groma to lay straight, cambered stone roads with drainage ditches.

items.question: How did a Roman hypocaust heat bathhouses like Aquae Sulis and wealthy villas?
items.answer: Hot air from a furnace flowed beneath raised floors resting on stacks of brick tiles (pilae)
items.explanation: Hypocaust central heating warmed mosaic floors and steaming bath rooms.

items.question: While rich leaders built mosaic villas like Fishbourne Palace, how did almost nine in ten Britons live?
items.answer: Farming in the countryside inside thatched roundhouses while paying Roman taxes
items.explanation: Most ordinary families in rural Britain continued living in roundhouses throughout the Roman era.

current_items.question: In what year did Emperor Honorius tell British towns they must defend themselves?
current_items.explanation: In AD 410, with Italy itself under attack, Emperor Honorius wrote that Rome could send no more troops to Britain.

current_items.question: Which raiders crossed the North Sea to attack eastern Britain around AD 400?
current_items.explanation: While Picts raided from Scotland and Scotti from Ireland, Angles and Saxons sailed across the North Sea.

current_items.question: Name two famous buried Roman silver treasures found centuries later in Suffolk.
current_items.answer: The Hoxne Hoard and the Mildenhall Treasure
current_items.explanation: Wealthy families buried chests of coins, spoons, and silver dishes underground for safekeeping and never returned.

current_items.question: What Latin word for a Roman fort gave towns like Manchester and Lancaster their names?
current_items.explanation: British place-names ending in -chester, -caster, or -cester mark the site of a Roman castra (fort).

current_items.question: Which two calendar months are named after Julius Caesar and Rome's first emperor Augustus?
current_items.explanation: Our 12-month Roman calendar still honours Julius Caesar (July) and Emperor Augustus (August).

narrative_blocks.title: Raiders on Every Coast & Leaving in AD 410
narrative_blocks.text:
[6.1] Around **AD 400**, after nearly four hundred years in Britain, the **Roman Empire** faced fierce attacks everywhere. **Picts** from Scotland, **Scotti** from Ireland, and seafaring **Angles and Saxons** raided Britain's coasts. Meanwhile, **Visigoth** [VIZ-ih-goth] armies invaded **Italy** and threatened **Rome** itself.

[6.2] Roman legions sailed away across the Channel to defend Italy. When worried British towns begged for help in **AD 410**, **Emperor Honorius** [hoh-NOR-ee-us] replied that Rome had no spare soldiers left, so **British towns must defend themselves**.

narrative_blocks.title: Buried Silver Treasure & Crumbling Bathhouses
narrative_blocks.text:
[6.3] Once the Roman army left Britain, fresh **Roman coins** stopped arriving to pay soldiers' **wages**. Busy town markets shrank and pottery workshops closed their doors. Nobody fixed leaky stone **aqueducts**, **hypocausts**, or **bathhouses**, so grand buildings slowly **crumbled** into silent ruins.

[6.4] Fearing coastal raiders, rich families buried wooden chests of gold coins, spoons, and silver plates underground in a secret **hoard**. Many owners never came home! Centuries later, **Suffolk** farmers ploughed up the glittering **Hoxne Hoard** [HOKS-un] and **Mildenhall Treasure**.

narrative_blocks.title: Roman Footprints Still Shaping Britain Today
narrative_blocks.text:
[6.5] Even after the legions left, Rome left a lasting **legacy** all around us today. **Londinium** grew into **London**, and straight modern **A-roads** follow old Roman highways. Town names ending in **-chester** or **-caster**, like Manchester and Lancaster, mark Roman army forts (**castra** [KAS-truh]).

[6.6] Every day we write with the **Latin** **ABC alphabet** and read **Roman numerals** (**I, V, X**) on clocks. Our **12-month calendar** names **July** and **August** after Roman leaders, and Rome brought **Christianity**, **apples**, **cabbages**, **rabbits**, and **stinging nettles**!

tasks.question: Read Zosimus's words beside Emperor Honorius's gold coin in Source A. Why couldn't Honorius send legions to Britain in AD 410?
tasks.starter: Looking closely at Source A, Emperor Honorius could not send fresh soldiers to defend Britain in AD 410 because...
hints: Identify Emperor Honorius on the gold coin and Zosimus’s account of AD 410.
Explain what crisis was happening closer to Rome as enemy armies like the Visigoths attacked Italy.

tasks.model_answer: Looking closely at Source A, Emperor Honorius could not send fresh soldiers to defend Britain in AD 410 because enemy armies such as the Visigoths were attacking Italy and Rome itself. With zero spare legions left, Honorius wrote telling British cities they must guard themselves against Pictish, Irish, and Saxon raiders.

tasks.title: 2. Historical Investigation
tasks.question: Why did the Roman army leave Britain around AD 410, and what happened to Roman coins and stone bathhouses afterwards?
tasks.starter: The Roman army marched away from Britain around AD 410 because the Roman Empire...
hints: Name the enemies attacking Britain (Picts, Scotti, Angles, and Saxons) AND the Visigoths attacking Italy and Rome itself.
Explain Emperor Honorius's AD 410 reply telling British towns they must defend themselves.
Trace the knock-on effect of soldiers leaving: why did stopping army wages make town markets shrink and bathhouses crumble?
tasks.model_answer: The Roman army marched away from Britain around AD 410 because the Roman Empire was under attack everywhere at once. While Picts from Scotland, Scotti from Ireland, and Angles and Saxons across the North Sea raided Britain, Visigoth armies invaded Italy and threatened Rome itself. Legions were called back to save Italy, and in AD 410 Emperor Honorius told British towns they must defend themselves. Without soldiers' wages arriving, new Roman coins disappeared, town workshops shut down, and leaky aqueducts, hypocausts, and stone bathhouses slowly crumbled into ruins.

tasks.question: Big Question: Why did the Roman army leave Britain around AD 410, and what did the Romans leave behind for us today?

hints: Include towns and travel: Londinium becoming London, -chester/-caster fort towns (from castra), and modern A-roads along straight Roman routes.

tasks.model_answer: Even though the Roman legions marched away in AD 410, Rome changed Britain forever by leaving behind a legacy we still use every single day. On our maps, Londinium grew into our capital city London, towns ending in -chester or -caster mark Roman forts (castra), and modern A-roads still follow straight Roman highways. Even more importantly, Rome gave us the Latin ABC alphabet we read and write with, Roman numerals (I, V, X) on clocks, the 12-month calendar including July and August, written laws, Christianity, and everyday foods and wildlife from apples and cabbages to rabbits and stinging nettles!

quiz.question: Which groups raided Roman Britain from Scotland, Ireland, and across the North Sea around AD 400?
quiz.q: Which groups raided Roman Britain from Scotland, Ireland, and across the North Sea around AD 400?
options: Picts, Scotti, and Angles and Saxons

quiz.a: Picts, Scotti, and Angles and Saxons
quiz.explanation: Around AD 400, Picts raided from Scotland, Scotti from Ireland, and Angles and Saxons sailed across the North Sea.

quiz.question: Why were Roman legions called away from Britain in the early fifth century?
quiz.q: Why were Roman legions called away from Britain in the early fifth century?

Because British winters had turned tropical
To defend Italy and Rome itself against invading armies like the Visigoths

quiz.question: In what year did Emperor Honorius send his famous reply telling British towns to defend themselves?
quiz.q: In what year did Emperor Honorius send his famous reply telling British towns to defend themselves?

Everyone in Britain must move to Rome
Hadrian's Wall would be rebuilt in marble

Picts from Scotland and Scotti from Ireland

Picts from Syria and Scotti from Gaul

Gold mines on the Moon closed down

quiz.a: There were no longer Roman soldiers in Britain receiving army wages

quiz.question: What happened to many Roman stone bathhouses, aqueducts, and hypocausts after AD 410?
quiz.q: What happened to many Roman stone bathhouses, aqueducts, and hypocausts after AD 410?

They were covered in solid gold
They were shipped brick by brick back to Italy
Nobody repaired them, so they slowly crumbled into overgrown ruins

options: To grow silver trees in their orchards
To hide their valuables safely from raiders, hoping to dig them up when danger passed
To pay taxes to Queen Boudicca
quiz.answer: To hide their valuables safely from raiders, hoping to dig them up when danger passed
quiz.a: To hide their valuables safely from raiders, hoping to dig them up when danger passed

quiz.question: What happened to town markets and pottery workshops in Britain once Roman army wages stopped arriving?
quiz.q: What happened to town markets and pottery workshops in Britain once Roman army wages stopped arriving?

Markets shrank rapidly and potters' workshops closed their doors
Potters began exporting millions of plates to China
Emperor Honorius paid every potter in solid gold

quiz.a: Markets shrank rapidly and potters' workshops closed their doors

quiz.q: What does a British town name ending in -chester or -caster (like Manchester or Lancaster) reveal?

It was founded by Julius Caesar's elephants
It grew on the site of a Roman fort (castra)

quiz.a: It grew on the site of a Roman fort (castra)

quiz.q: Which two months of our 12-month calendar are named after Julius Caesar and Emperor Augustus?
